title: Simplicial mapping components compute localized morphisms
statement: Use model categories, weak factorization systems, functorial factorizations, cofibrant and fibrant objects as defined in [lem-coef-simplicial-boundary-collapse-test], simplicial tensors and cotensors as defined in [def-coef-simplicial-tensor-cotensor], and the Kan model structure of [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper]. Enlarge universes so the categories and localizations below exist as ordinary categories. A simplicial model category means a model category enriched, tensored and cotensored over simplicial sets, in which for each cofibration $a:A\to B$ and fibration $p:X\to Y$ the corner map $\operatorname{Map}(B,X)\to\operatorname{Map}(A,X)\times_{\operatorname{Map}(A,Y)}\operatorname{Map}(B,Y)$ is a Kan fibration, trivial if $a$ or $p$ is weak. Let $\mathcal M$ be a simplicial model category. Write $q:\mathcal M\to\mathcal L=\mathcal M[W^{-1}]$ for the ordinary category obtained from finite composable strings of ordinary arrows and formal inverses of weak equivalences, modulo the composition, identity and inverse relations. Assume the ordinary bifibrant localization and saturation conclusions of [lem-coef-simplicial-bifibrant-localization]. For every cofibrant $P$ and fibrant $Y$, sending a vertex $f:P\to Y$ to $q(f)$ induces a bijection $\pi_0\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal M}(P,Y)\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal L}(qP,qY)$. This bijection is natural for all actual arrows between cofibrant sources and between fibrant targets, and respects composition whenever both the source and target conditions hold. It is the bijection induced by the actual localization functor, not merely an abstract bijection of sets.

proof.text: Factor $P\to *$ as a trivial cofibration $i:P\to A$ followed by a fibration $A\to *$, and factor $0\to Y$ as a cofibration $0\to B$ followed by a trivial fibration $p:B\to Y$. These factorizations exist by the two weak factorization systems in [lem-coef-simplicial-boundary-collapse-test]. The objects $A$ and $B$ are bifibrant: $A$ is fibrant by construction and $B$ is cofibrant by construction; $0\to A$ is the composite of the cofibrations $0\to P$ and $i$, and $B\to *$ is the composite of the fibrations $p$ and $Y\to *$. For completeness, closure of either lifting class under twofold composition needs only two fillers: for a composite of left-class maps, fill against the first map using the prescribed map out of the second object's target, then fill against the second; the dual two-fillers argument proves closure of the right class. Thus the indicated composites belong to the required classes. No properness hypothesis is used.

proof.text:
For any objects $U,V$, the simplicial sets $\operatorname{Map}(U,*)$ and $\operatorname{Map}(0,V)$ are terminal. Indeed, by the representing isomorphisms of [def-coef-simplicial-tensor-cotensor], their $n$-simplices identify respectively with $\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta^n\otimes U,*)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}(0,V^{\Delta^n})$, each a singleton by the ordinary terminal and initial universal properties. The simplicial operators between singleton sets are unique. Consequently the corner maps in the assumed simplicial model axiom for $(i,B\to *)$ and $(0\to P,p)$ identify respectively with
$$i^*:\operatorname{Map}(A,B)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Map}(P,B),\qquad p_*:\operatorname{Map}(P,B)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Map}(P,Y).$$

source.place: Extracted mapping-localization prerequisite, identification of the two corner-map targets with mapping sets

proof.text:
Both maps displayed in step 2 are trivial Kan fibrations. For the first, $i$ is a trivial cofibration and $B\to *$ is a fibration; for the second, $0\to P$ is a cofibration and $p$ is a trivial fibration. These are precisely the hypotheses of the assumed simplicial model axiom. A trivial Kan fibration is in particular a weak homotopy equivalence. By the definition of weak homotopy equivalence in [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper], its realization induces a bijection on path components. Applying this twice gives the bijection
$$r=\pi_0(p_*)\,\pi_0(i^*):\pi_0\operatorname{Map}(A,B)\xrightarrow{\sim}\pi_0\operatorname{Map}(P,Y),\qquad [h]\longmapsto[p\circ h\circ i].$$
The formula follows from the definition of precomposition and postcomposition in the enrichment.

source.place: Extracted mapping-localization prerequisite, the two trivial mapping fibrations and their component bijections

proof.text:
Use the assumed ordinary bifibrant-localization conclusion of [lem-coef-simplicial-bifibrant-localization]. Its equivalence $H\to\mathcal L$ sends the vertex class of an actual arrow $h:A\to B$ to $q(h)$. Since $A,B$ are bifibrant, its map on these Hom sets is the bijection
$$b:\pi_0\operatorname{Map}(A,B)\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal L}(qA,qB),\qquad[h]\longmapsto q(h).$$
Here the Hom-set inverse is supplied by a quasi-inverse of the equivalence and its comparison isomorphisms. The finite-string localization $q:\mathcal M\to\mathcal L$ inverts $i,p$, since they are weak equivalences. Hence
$$c:\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal L}(qA,qB)\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal L}(qP,qY),\qquad u\longmapsto q(p)\circ u\circ q(i)$$
has inverse $v\mapsto q(p)^{-1}\circ v\circ q(i)^{-1}$. We obtain a well-defined bijection $\theta=c\circ b\circ r^{-1}$ from $\pi_0\operatorname{Map}(P,Y)$ to the desired localized Hom set. It remains to identify it on every vertex, rather than merely exhibit an abstract bijection.

source.place: Extracted mapping-localization prerequisite, bifibrant comparison and transport along the two inverted replacements

proof.text:
Let $f:P\to Y$ be any vertex. Lift $f$ through the trivial fibration $p$ using the cofibration $0\to P$: the square with top $0\to B$ and bottom $f$ gives $g:P\to B$ with $pg=f$. Extend $g$ across the trivial cofibration $i$ using the fibration $B\to *$: the square with top $g$ and bottom the unique $A\to *$ gives $h:A\to B$ with $hi=g$. Both fillers are exactly the lifting properties in [lem-coef-simplicial-boundary-collapse-test]. Therefore $phi=f$ as actual arrows, not merely up to homotopy. Step 3 gives $r([h])=[f]$, so step 4 yields
$$\theta([f])=c(b([h]))=q(p)\circ q(h)\circ q(i)=q(phi)=q(f).$$
Thus sending vertices to their actual localized arrows is constant on each component, and its induced map is the bijection $\theta$. This computation also makes the bijection independent of every replacement and filler choice. In particular there is no prior assumption that $q$ identifies simplicial paths between non-bifibrant objects.

source.place: Extracted mapping-localization prerequisite, verification that the comparison is induced by the actual localization functor

proof.text:
For an actual arrow $a:P'\to P$ between cofibrant objects and an actual arrow $d:Y\to Y'$ between fibrant objects, enriched precomposition and postcomposition induce the map $[f]\mapsto[dfa]$ on components. The enrichment and its identification of underlying arrows with vertices are part of [def-coef-simplicial-tensor-cotensor]. Every component contains a vertex, so the identity
$$\theta_{P',Y'}([dfa])=q(dfa)=q(d)\circ\theta_{P,Y}([f])\circ q(a)$$
proves the asserted naturality for all such actual arrows, with no weak-equivalence restriction on $a,d$. For composable vertices $f:P\to Y$ and $g:Y\to Z$, whenever $P,Y$ are cofibrant and $Y,Z$ are fibrant so the three bijections apply, enriched composition on components is $([g],[f])\mapsto[gf]$. Hence $\theta_{P,Z}([gf])=q(gf)=\theta_{Y,Z}([g])\circ\theta_{P,Y}([f])$. The identity vertex goes to the identity under $q$ as well. This proves all composition and identity assertions.
